content.title: Semantic HTML Is Free Accessibility
content.hook: In the previous module, you learned that HTML elements have meaning. Accessibility gives that idea another consequence: meaningful HTML is not only cleaner. It gives the browser useful information about what each control or piece of content is.
content.context: Use the element that already means what you need. A button should be a button. A link should be a link. A heading should be a heading. A paragraph should be a paragraph.
goals: Use native HTML elements for their intended jobs and recognize why meaningful elements provide useful behavior and information to browsers and assistive technology.

content.question: A piece of text takes the user to another page. Which element is the direct semantic choice?

feedback.correct: A link represents navigation to another resource. Use a link for navigation instead of making another element pretend to be a link.
feedback.incorrect: A link represents navigation to another resource. Use a link for navigation instead of making another element pretend to be a link.

content.question: A control performs an action on the current page. Which element is the direct semantic choice?

feedback.correct: A button represents an action. The browser already knows useful things about native buttons.
feedback.incorrect: A button represents an action. The browser already knows useful things about native buttons.

activities.title: What you get from native controls

content.title: What you get from native controls
content.text:
Native controls come with expected browser behavior and meaning. For example, buttons can be reached and activated with the keyboard, and links are recognized as navigation controls.

You are not “doing less” by using the native element. You are choosing a foundation that already carries useful behavior.

content.question: The previous line is intended to be a button. What is the strongest repair?

options.text: Keep the div and add more CSS until it looks like a button.
Replace the div with a button element.

feedback.correct: Start with the correct semantic element. Styling cannot give a generic container the complete meaning and default interaction behavior of a native button.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the correct semantic element. Styling cannot give a generic container the complete meaning and default interaction behavior of a native button.

content.question: Which rule should guide this work?

options.text: Use the element that looks closest to the design.
Use the element with the correct meaning for the job.
Use div for everything so the CSS stays consistent.
Use the most complicated element available.

feedback.correct: Meaning first. Visual styling comes later.
feedback.incorrect: Meaning first. Visual styling comes later.
